To distinguish between M18, M11, M9, and M12, we must orthogonally perturb the concentrations that drive their respective deactivation rates. 
1. By using a low substrate concentration (S=0.5) compared to all previous runs (where S >= 1.0), we will significantly decrease the ratio of `[S][cat]` to `[cat]`. This will strongly differentiate M11 (deactivation ~ `[S][cat]`) from M9 (deactivation ~ `[cat]`).
2. The low substrate concentration also ensures that `[catS]` remains relatively low. Since M18's deactivation scales with `[catS]^2`, its deactivation rate will drop quadratically, separating it from the linear dependencies of M11 and M9.
3. By introducing a moderate initial product concentration (P=0.2), we establish a baseline deactivation rate for M12 (deactivation ~ `[P][cat]`) right from the start of the reaction. As the reaction progresses and P increases to 0.7, M12 will show a distinct accelerating deactivation profile compared to M9, which depends only on `[cat]`.
This specific combination (S=0.5, cat=0.05, P=0.2) creates a kinetic regime where the deactivation rates of the top four models will diverge dramatically.
</hypothesis>
